author: Gašper Ažman

evidence.note: In P2826R0 (2023), Gašper Ažman proposed a function definition whose body is a constant expression evaluating to a function pointer (e.g., `auto f(U) = &g;`) that substitutes the target function at a selected call site. The R4 paper has replaced that mechanism entirely: instead of declaring `int takes_int(int) = &takes_long;` it declares expression aliases with `using declarator = (expression);`, substituting an arbitrary target expression rather than a pointer to a function.
evidence.title: P2826R0: Function Aliases
evidence.what_changed: R0 proposed `auto f(U) = &g;` — a declaration-time constant expression yielding a function pointer that replaces the selected call. R4 replaces that design with `using declarator = (expression);`, an AST rewrite of the call to an arbitrary target expression, dropping the pointer-to-function constant-expression model; the later revision also drops the R0 use cases of programmable =delete/null pointers and virtual-function dispatch.

evidence.note: P2826R2 (2024) still proposed the older mechanism: a function definition whose body is a constant expression designating a target function (e.g., `auto g(unsigned) = f;`). R4 replaced this with expression aliases — `using declarator = (expression);` — in which the parameters are in scope and any target expression is substituted at the call site, not a declaration-time function pointer.
evidence.title: P2826R2: Replacement functions (later Expression Aliases)
evidence.what_changed: R2 used `auto name(params) = constant-expression;` with the constant expression designating a single target function or member function, and still allowed null targets for programmable =delete and virtual-function dispatch. R4 drops the pointer/reference-to-function target model and instead declares `using name(params) = (expression);`, rewriting the call to an arbitrary target expression with parameters in scope; the programmable-delete and virtual use cases are gone.

evidence.note: P2826R3 already had the `using declarator = (expression);` expression-alias syntax of R4, but treated an ill-formed substituted target expression as a hard error and said aliases "do not introduce a new scope." R4 adopts a "SFINAE-at-call-site" model where substitution failure is a SFINAE failure in SFINAE contexts, and lays out hygiene, linkage, AST-transform, lifetime, and recursion rules.
evidence.title: P2826R3: Expression Aliases
evidence.what_changed: Between R3 and R4 the author changed the error model: R3 said an invalid substituted target expression is a hard error and that expression aliases do not introduce a scope; R4 makes the substituted expression SFINAE-able at the call site, removes the "no new scope/hygienic substitution" framing in favor of AST transformation after selection, and adds explicit rules for no linkage, lifetime extension of temporaries, recursion via if consteval, and access control.

position: Gašper Ažman has consistently advocated, from P2826R0 through R4, for a C++ language feature that adds an entry to an overload set which is rewritten at the call site to another target without an intervening forwarding function, with the stated goals of avoiding template bloat, preserving copy elision, and removing library-defined dispatch from call stacks. In R0 he proposed `auto f(U) = &g;`, a declaration-time constant expression yielding a function or member-function pointer to substitute. By R3/R4 he had replaced that model with expression aliases, `using declarator = (expression);`, which substitute the parameter expressions directly into an arbitrary target expression; along the way he dropped the earlier programmable-`=delete`/null-target and virtual-dispatch use cases. Between R3 and R4 he also changed the error model from "ill-formed target expression is a hard error" to "SFINAE-at-call-site," making substitution failures part of the immediate context, and added explicit lifetime, linkage, recursion, and access-control rules.
recommendation: P2826R4 proposes a new C++ entity called an expression alias, declared with syntax `using declarator = (expression);`, which rewrites a function call to a different expression without a forwarding layer, avoiding template bloat, preserving copy elision, and removing library-defined dispatch from call stacks.
title: Expression Aliases
